tasks.short: Verify new arrivals' identity, enter details and charges, record property, update charges and dates as they change and check the headcount list.

steps.what: Officer checks the identity of new arrivals against transfer papers
Officer types prisoners' identification, charges and court dates from the papers into the prison system
Officer photographs the prisoner and lists their property: on paper today, in the prison system after the change
Officer updates records when charges, court dates or release dates change by letter
Officer checks the daily headcount list against the records by hand

tasks.design: The arrival record in the prison information system ({OPS_SYSTEM}) is filled from the electronic transfer of the police and prosecution, and the officer confirms identity with the fingerprint check and corrects the fields. Later changes in charges and court dates arrive as messages from the justice chain for the officer to accept, and the headcount view lists only differences; property and photos stay manual.
tasks.previous_blocker: Details arrived on paper and were retyped; changes came by letter.
tasks.enabler_now: Justice chain partners exchange case data electronically.
tasks.still_hard: Wrong data in the chain flows straight in; identity must still be confirmed in person.
tasks.human_edge: Noticing that the person in front of you is not who the papers say.
tasks.altitude: The officer confirms records instead of typing them.

reach.learn: Whether chain messages end late release-date changes.

evidence.claim: Justice chain partners can exchange case data electronically so records need not be retyped.
Prisoner records are justice data with strict access and retention rules.
AI for reoffending risk or evidence reliability is high-risk; this design uses no AI.

assumptions: Boundary: from arrival to the daily headcount; release is outside.
Input contract: transfer data sent by police and prosecution through the chain exchange; field mapping kept by the prison's information manager; fallback is the paper transfer file.
Information manager time is outside the officer's savings.

Property records and photos stay manual and keep their full time. s1 keeps 60 because the fingerprint check replaces comparing papers and the officer still confirms the person; s2 keeps 20 for arrivals without electronic transfer and for corrections; s4 keeps 40 for accepting or querying chain messages; s5 keeps 50 because only differences are listed and resolving them stays.
unknowns: Which chain messages the prison system can receive.
research_questions: Do record errors fall when data are not retyped?

already_counted.description: Officer checks the prefilled arrival record.
Officer accepts or queries chain update messages.

incremental.description: Officer reports mismatches in chain data.
Information manager maintains the chain field mapping.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: about half of arrivals and changes come from partners without electronic transfer, so they are still typed (31.0); high: most arrivals come through the chain exchange (47.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Sign out keys and radio, operate doors, cameras and intercoms, use radio and metal detector, read the unit schedule on the computer, and report broken equipment.

steps.what: Officer signs out keys and radio at shift start in the paper key register
Officer uses nondisciplinary equipment such as door controls, cameras and intercoms from the unit panel
Officer uses the radio and metal detector during movements and searches
Officer uses the computer to read the unit schedule and notes at shift start
Officer describes the broken equipment and the fault: on a paper form today, on a short form on the unit computer after the change
Officer checks the fault report before it goes: the equipment, location, fault and urgency
Officer submits the checked fault report to facilities: by taking the paper form over today, by sending it to the facilities helpdesk after the change

tasks.design: An electronic key cabinet opens with the officer's pass and records which keys and radio each officer takes and returns, so the paper key register goes. The prison information system ({OPS_SYSTEM}) opens each shift with one unit overview of appointments, visits and alerts instead of scrolling notes. The officer describes broken equipment on a short form on the unit computer, checks it and sends it to the facilities helpdesk ({HELPDESK}) instead of carrying a paper form over. Operating doors, cameras, radio and detectors stays with the officer.
tasks.previous_blocker: Keys were signed out on paper, notes read by scrolling and faults reported on paper forms.
tasks.enabler_now: Electronic key cabinets, overview screens and helpdesk forms are standard.
tasks.still_hard: Key cabinets need a fallback when the system is down.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing from the morning mood on the unit that today needs extra care.

evidence.claim: Electronic key cabinets can record who takes and returns each key.
A key log per officer can observe staff and needs works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: one shift's use of keys, radio, panel, detectors and computer; unit logs, movement records and requests are separate tasks.
Input contract: key cabinet and overview screen set up by the prison; fallback is the paper register and notes.
The key log is used for key control, not to rate officers.

Operating the panel, radio and detectors, describing faults (a first record) and checking the report keep their full time. s1 keeps 40 for taking and returning keys at the cabinet; s4 keeps 70 because reading the overview stays; submitting keeps 25.

approvals.approved_version: The fault report with equipment, location, fault and urgency exactly as checked by the officer in s5c, submitted once to the facilities helpdesk queue; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: spare keys and night shifts still go through the paper register (9.5); high: all keys and radios sit in the cabinet (14.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Attend practical training, do e-learning, enrol in required courses, hand in certificates and arrange shifts around training.

steps.what: Officer attends practical training in self-defence, first aid and fire safety
Officer completes e-learning modules
Officer finds and enrols in required training after reminders from the trainer
Trainer records the officer's completion of practical training in the learning system
Officer hands paper certificates to the training office today; after the change only certificates from outside courses are uploaded
Officer swaps shifts with colleagues to attend training

tasks.design: The {LMS} assigns each officer's required courses with due dates and records completion: e-learning by itself, practical training by the trainer's mark, and outside certificates uploaded by the officer; and booked training days are placed in the roster so swaps are rarely needed. Practical training and e-learning stay as they are.
tasks.previous_blocker: Required training was tracked by the trainer on lists and certificates were handed in on paper.
tasks.enabler_now: Learning systems assign required courses and record completion; rosters can hold training days.
tasks.still_hard: Staff shortages make training days hard to release.
tasks.human_edge: Practising a restraint with colleagues until it is safe for everyone.

reach.learn: Whether automatic records show overdue training earlier.

evidence.claim: Learning systems assign required courses with due dates and record completion.
Training records per officer are personnel data; using them to monitor staff needs works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from required course to recorded completion; course content is outside.
Input contract: required courses per role set by the training officer; roster kept by the planner; fallback is lists and paper.
Planner, trainer (s4t, share 1) and training officer time is outside the officer's savings.

Attending training and e-learning keep their full time. s3 keeps 40 because courses are assigned and choosing a date stays; s4 keeps 20 for uploading outside certificates; s5 keeps 60 because booked days are in the roster and some swaps remain.
unknowns: Training days per officer per year.

incremental.description: Officer checks assigned courses in the learning system.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: many certificates come from outside courses and the roster does not hold training days (11.3); high: most training is recorded in the system and placed in the roster (15.8).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Notice tension, step in, talk with the inmates to settle the dispute, decide on measures and write the incident report.

steps.what: Officer notices tension between inmates and steps in
Officer talks with the inmates to settle disputes between them
Officer decides on measures within the rules or reports to the unit head
Officer writes the incident report in free text

tasks.design: The incident report in the prison information system ({OPS_SYSTEM}) gets fixed fields (who, where, when, type, measure) prefilled from the unit log, and the officer writes the account in their own words. Spotting, settling and deciding stay fully with the officer; no AI drafts the account, because a trial found AI-drafted police reports were not written faster. The incident report belongs to the task on recording incidents, 33-3012.00:15255, and is priced there; settling disputes and deciding measures do not change.
tasks.previous_blocker: Reports were written entirely in free text.
tasks.enabler_now: Records systems support structured fields prefilled from logs.
tasks.still_hard: The account must be the officer's own; it can lead to disciplinary measures.
tasks.human_edge: Calming two angry men before anyone gets hurt.

reach.learn: Whether structured fields make reports easier to compare.

evidence.claim: A randomised trial found AI-drafted police reports were not written faster; one department's own figure claimed 8 against 23 minutes.
Incident reports can lead to disciplinary measures, so the account must be the officer's own.

assumptions: Boundary: from noticing tension to the incident report; disciplinary hearings are outside.
Input contract: report fields set by the unit head; unit log entries from the shift; fallback is free text.
s4 is part of recording incidents, which sibling task 33-3012.00:15255 covers; its saving is counted there, so s4 keeps its full time here.
research_questions: Do structured fields make incident patterns visible?

incremental.description: No upkeep in this task; learning the structured incident fields is counted with sibling task 33-3012.00:15255.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: No saving in this task: the only changed step belongs to sibling task 33-3012.00:15255.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The correctional officer keeps supervision, de-escalation and judgement; retyping, logs and paper training records shrink.
role.ambitious_version: An officer who spends the shift on the unit with prisoners, not behind the computer.
